Scene

One strip, every lane: season re-ink, projector gain and tint, sweep, wind, rain, trace glow, and the visitors — motes and fireflies, plus monarchs, meadow butterflies and moths, each one hashed whole from its seed. Live the day walks the strip by itself. Sliders below still override anything, until the next scene.

Projector

Light only is what the projector should emit onto the real printed wall: the print supplies the pigment, the beam carries only the living light — critters, rain, glow, sweep. Project goes fullscreen and applies the saved corner warp; Esc leaves it again (from fullscreen that reads as two presses — the first one is the browser's), or click the Exit chip that fades in whenever you move the mouse. Calibrate shows draggable corners, the tile grid, and the camera tools — drag the projected corners onto the wall, then slide the print until the grid sits on the printed seams. Pop out opens the operator console for a second screen: camera, dials and snap live there while the wall shows only the art.

A landing is bioluminescence: a butterfly settling on a bloom lights it amber, a moth moonlit blue — the glow each species already wears — eased in, held, eased out. A white bloom takes the fill colours over its whole matte, carrying its own relief (the print’s broad light and shadow); a pink bloom’s pigment swallows a fill, so it takes the outline colours instead: its silhouette and strongest petal contours as a glowing line, built from the outline dials. Butterflies and moths each carry their own three colour pairs here, all in view: the fill, the outline, and the halo the critter wears in flight (which the dust borrows). Colours are HSL: lightness is the projector operator’s slider. Two critters on one bloom cross-fade; a held landing lets go when the last one leaves. Touch: press a lit bloom and its light comes apart into sparks from the touch point outward while you hold — each spark carries exactly the light of the petals it left (which go dark and stay dark until the bloom is lit again), leaves with the stroke’s momentum and a push from the touch, then drifts on the wall’s wind, rises a little, coils, and cools. Splash density sets how many sparks share the light, Splash energy how long they burn. Everything here rides in presets and share links.

How it moves

The print holds still. Field-tested: the flowers do not need to move — they are printed on the wall. The critters, the rain, the glow and the sweep are the experience, and every one of them still knows exactly where the flowers are: the faces steer the visitors, and the depth weave slips particles behind the printed blooms through the paper mask.

Every flower has a face. The printed heads are not orthogonal — each tips toward its own direction and is foreshortened by its tilt — so every one carries a face: center, radius, facing and tilt, kind and color. A critter lands on a site laid in that flower’s own plane — on the rays, the pad or the near lip, never the pistil — lies along it, head to the center, and its wings fold up toward the flower’s normal: closed wings vanish to a line on a face-on bloom and stand up in full profile on a cup seen from the side. Butterflies take the pinks and the whites alike and pump their wings half-open as they feed; moths settle flat and keep to the pale night flowers. Buds have nowhere to land. #FLOWERS opens the editor to tune the faces on the wall.

Nobody flies parallel to the wall. In the air the body has three axes too: it banks into every turn, flutters about its own axis with each stroke, bobs its nose with the beat and drifts its pitch so the wing plane is never long parallel to the eye — a real butterfly’s flight is roll-heavy; a moth flies steadier; a glider sails flat. The same fold, seen from where you stand. And it has depth: in the open a critter weaves between behind the print — smaller, dimmer, eclipsed by the printed blooms — and well in front of it, larger; it comes back to the print’s own plane for every landing.

Rain knows the print. The wall’s silhouette ships as a signed distance field, so a drop lands on the drawn edge of the print, runs down that surface, beads, merges, and drips from the rim — the water moves; the flowers never do.

Water bends light, and gravity bends water. Every settled bead paints a lens into a displacement map, and one filter over the composed wall refracts the actual print through it — the pigment genuinely warps under each drop, scaled by the Drop size dial. No drop is a circle: mass sags each bead into an egg (tension holds the small ones rounder), a drop hanging at a leaf’s rim necks into a pendant before it lets go, and sliding drops jiggle and tow a wet wake. The bead itself is drawn in projector terms: light added for the specular and the gathered crescent, light withheld for the rim and body shadow — and its lens wears the same sagged silhouette.

Drops live together, windshield rules. A field of static condensation textures the wall; heavy sliders carry the motion — each one absorbs every droplet in its swept path, growing as it goes, shedding a dotted trail of micro-drops that costs it mass, so it starves, stalls, gathers and lurches again. Rain impacts feed the field; a dry spell evaporates it.
